title: The Burning Bush and the Name of God
summary: While shepherding his father-in-law's flock near Horeb, the mountain of God, Moses sees a bush that burns without burning up. God calls to him from the bush, tells him he is on holy ground, and announces that he has seen his people's affliction and has come down to rescue them, sending Moses to Pharaoh. When Moses protests, God promises his presence, reveals his name, I AM WHO I AM, the LORD, and foretells Pharaoh's resistance, God's mighty acts, and Israel's departure with the wealth of Egypt.
story:
At the end of Exodus 2 God heard Israel's groaning, remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saw the Israelites, and took notice (2:23-25). This chapter is the answer, and it picks up those very verbs: God has seen, has heard, and knows (3:7). Moses, once raised in Pharaoh's house and then a fugitive after killing an Egyptian, has spent long years as a shepherd in Midian; Stephen's speech counts forty (Acts 7:30), and Moses is eighty when he stands before Pharaoh (7:7). Now, at the mountain where Israel will later receive the covenant, he meets the God of his ancestors.

God introduces himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, tying this new rescue to the promises of Genesis, and then lays out the plan of the whole book in advance. Moses will go to Pharaoh; Pharaoh will refuse; God will strike Egypt with wonders; the people will come out, not empty-handed, and worship God on this very mountain (verse 12). The promise of a land flowing with milk and honey looks further ahead, past Exodus, to the conquest. Moses' reluctance begins here with “Who am I?” and runs through five objections in all (3:11, 3:13, 4:1, 4:10, 4:13) before he finally returns to Egypt. The man who once tried to deliver his people on his own initiative and was asked who made him a ruler (2:14) is now sent by God, and Stephen draws exactly that contrast (Acts 7:35).
historical:
Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai; Deuteronomy prefers Horeb and Exodus mostly Sinai, and 1 Kings 19:8 calls it “Horeb, the mountain of God” when Elijah flees there. Its location is not known with certainty. Christian tradition since the fourth century has placed it at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula. The pilgrim Egeria, who traveled there in the early 380s, describes a church standing beside a bush in a garden at the foot of the mountain, and between 548 and 565 the emperor Justinian built the fortified monastery now called Saint Catherine's around that spot; its Chapel of the Burning Bush still claims the site. Other proposals include peaks in the northern Sinai, Har Karkom in the Negev, where Emmanuel Anati found hundreds of ancient cult sites over decades of survey (though its main period of activity appears to be well before any proposed date of the exodus), and Jebel al-Lawz in northwest Arabia, argued on the ground that Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba. Paul places “Mount Sinai in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25), but the Roman province of Arabia and the older Greek use of the name could include the Sinai Peninsula, so the phrase does not settle the question.

Midian was the region east of the Gulf of Aqaba in northwest Arabia, though Midianites also appear as traders ranging far to the north and west (Genesis 37:28). Moses' father-in-law is here called Jethro, “the priest of Midian” (in 2:18 he is Reuel, and Judges 1:16 and 4:11 connect Moses' in-laws with the Kenites). Scholars have long noticed that Israel's God is connected in Scripture with the south: poems speak of the LORD coming from Seir, Edom, Teman, and Paran (Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4; Habakkuk 3:3). Egyptian evidence adds a striking detail. A topographical list on a column of Amenhotep III's temple at Soleb in Nubia (fourteenth century BC) names ‘the land of the Shasu of Yhw’, the Shasu being seminomads of the southern Levant, beside ‘the land of the Shasu of Seir’; a similar list appears under Ramesses II at Amarah West. It is the earliest known occurrence outside the Bible of a name that looks like YHWH, attached to a group in just the region where Exodus places Moses. What that means is debated (see the second hard question).

Which Pharaoh Moses would face depends on the date of the exodus, a question set out in the introduction to Exodus: those who follow 1 Kings 6:1 place it in the fifteenth century BC, in the reign of Thutmose III or Amenhotep II, while many others place it in the thirteenth century under Ramesses II, whose Delta capital appears as Rameses in 1:11. The chapter itself names no king.

The peoples listed in verses 8 and 17, Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, are a standard biblical roll of the inhabitants of Canaan. The Hittites named here are probably groups in Canaan known by that name, as in Genesis 23, rather than the great Hittite empire of Anatolia; the Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it (2 Samuel 5:6-9). The phrase a land flowing with milk and honey, used some twenty times in the Old Testament, describes rich pasture for goats and sheep and abundant sweetness. The Hebrew word for honey (devash) can mean both bee honey (Judges 14:8) and syrup from dates or grapes, and the Egyptian Story of Sinuhe, a Middle Kingdom tale, praises a land called Yaa in Syria-Palestine for its figs, grapes, wine, honey, olives, and cattle in terms very like these. Beekeeping in Israel itself is attested at Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley, where Amihai Mazar in 2007 excavated some 180 clay hives of the tenth and ninth centuries BC, the earliest apiary yet excavated in the ancient Near East.
cultural:
Taking off one's sandals was a sign of reverence and of a servant's place before a master. Joshua is told the same thing before the commander of the LORD's army (Joshua 5:15), and Israel's priests, whose clothing is described in detail in Exodus 28, are never given footwear; later Jewish tradition held that they served barefoot in the sanctuary. The ground was holy not because of the place but because of the presence there. Hiding one's face before God (verse 6) reflects the conviction stated in Exodus 33:20, “no one can see Me and live”, and Moses who hides his face here will later ask to see God's glory (33:18).

Shepherding was humble work, and Genesis notes that shepherds were detestable to the Egyptians (Genesis 46:34). Moses tending another man's flock recalls Jacob serving Laban, and Israel's later leaders were taken from the same trade (Psalm 78:70-72). The elders of Israel (verse 16) were the heads of families and clans who spoke for the people, and the chapter assumes that even under slavery Israel kept this structure of leadership.

In the ancient world a name expressed character and made a relationship possible. To know a god's name was to be able to call on him, and some traditions imagined that knowing a hidden name gave power over its owner: an Egyptian myth tells how Isis tricked the sun god Ra into revealing his secret name so that she could share his power. Moses' question, “What is His name?” (verse 13), asks what this God will prove to be for a people who have known him only as the God of their fathers. The answer both gives a name and refuses to hand God over to human control.

The request to Pharaoh for a three-day trip into the wilderness to sacrifice (verse 18) was a familiar kind of request. A limestone ostracon in the British Museum (EA 5634), a register of absences kept for the royal tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina in the fortieth year of Ramesses II, lists days when men were away from work, some of them for making an offering to a god. Moses is also told to speak of “the LORD, the God of the Hebrews”, the name Israel used for itself before foreigners (5:3; 7:16).

Finally, verses 21-22 describe a neighborly custom. The women are to ask their Egyptian neighbors, and even women lodging in their own houses, for silver and gold jewelry and clothing. Such gifts were portable wealth. Later law required that a released slave not be sent away empty-handed (Deuteronomy 15:13-15), and the same Hebrew word, reqam (‘empty’), appears in verse 21.
literary:
The chapter follows the pattern of a biblical call narrative. Norman Habel (Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft 77, 1965) identified six elements: a divine confrontation (verses 1-3), an introductory word (4-9), a commission (10), an objection (11), a reassurance (12a), and a sign (12b). The same pattern shapes the calls of Gideon (Judges 6), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1), and, with variations, Isaiah (Isaiah 6). Here the pattern is stretched: Moses' objections do not stop at one but continue into chapter 4, and the dialogue becomes a portrait of a reluctant prophet whom God will not release.

The verb see (ra'ah) drives the opening. The angel ‘let himself be seen’ (verse 2); Moses saw; he resolves to turn aside and see this great sight (verse 3); the LORD saw that he turned aside (verse 4); and God says, literally, ‘seeing, I have seen’ the affliction of his people (verse 7). Moses looks at a wonder, and discovers that he is the one being looked at, and that God has been looking at Israel all along. God's speech in verses 7-10 is a string of first-person verbs, I have seen, I have heard, I know, I have come down to rescue, and then, surprisingly, “I am sending you.” The rescue is wholly God's act and yet it will be carried out by a man.

The two objections that frame the name are built on the pronoun and the verb to be. Moses asks, ‘Who am I (mi anokhi)?’ God answers not with praise of Moses but with himself: ‘I will be (ehyeh) with you’ (verse 12). Two verses later ehyeh becomes the name itself (verse 14). The word the chapter uses for the bush, seneh, occurs only here and in Deuteronomy 33:16 and sounds like Sinai, and the fire in the bush anticipates the fire on the mountain in Exodus 19:18. Verses 16-22 then preview the book: the elders will listen (4:29-31), Pharaoh will refuse (chapter 5), God will stretch out his hand (chapters 7 to 12), and Israel will leave with Egypt's silver and gold (12:35-36).

Source critics have long divided the chapter between two strands, one using the name YHWH and one using Elohim (verse 4 uses both in a single sentence), and have compared its revelation of the name with a parallel priestly account in 6:2-8. Brevard Childs (The Book of Exodus, 1974) accepted a history of composition but argued that the final form is a deliberate whole and should be read as one, and many narrative critics read the change of names as a move from the personal name to the more general title rather than a seam.

outline.t: The bush that burns and is not consumed
God has seen his people's affliction and sends Moses
“Who am I?” and the promise of God's presence
Instructions for the elders and Pharaoh, and what will follow

doctrines.note: God reveals himself as I AM WHO I AM and gives his personal name, YHWH, “the LORD”, calling it “My name forever” (verse 15). The name is tied at once to a history: the LORD is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God is known by who he is and by what he has promised and done, and the name makes relationship possible without making God manageable.

Christian theology has drawn the doctrine of God's self-existence, often called aseity, partly from verse 14: God is not caused, completed, or sustained by anything outside himself. The same chapter shows that this God is not remote: he sees affliction, hears cries, and knows sufferings (verse 7), so that his independence and his compassion are revealed together.

The bush burns without being consumed, and the ground around it becomes holy (verse 5), the first time the noun holiness appears in the Bible. Holiness is God's own set-apart purity, which makes the ordinary places he enters holy and sets limits on how people approach him. Yet the holy God speaks and comes near to rescue.

God names himself three times as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (verses 6, 15, 16) and uses the very words Joseph left with Israel, ‘I have surely attended to you’ (verse 16; Genesis 50:24). The exodus is not a new idea but the keeping of an old oath, which is why 2:24 says God remembered his covenant.

“I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians” (verse 8). Salvation in Exodus begins with God's initiative, moved by his people's suffering and his covenant promises. It is rescue from a real oppressor into a real place, and its goal is worship: the people are brought out to serve God on his mountain (verse 12).

words.note: YHWH, the personal name of God, printed LORD in small capitals in most English Bibles. It is by far the most frequent name for God in the Old Testament, occurring about 6,800 times. Its form looks like a third person of the verb hayah (‘he is’ or ‘he will be’), and the chapter links it to God's first-person ehyeh (‘I am’ or ‘I will be’) in verse 14; lexicons such as HALOT discuss whether it is a simple or a causative form. By the last centuries before Christ Jews had largely stopped pronouncing it and read Adonai (‘Lord’) instead, and the Septuagint rendered it kyrios. The reconstruction Yahweh rests partly on Greek transcriptions in Clement of Alexandria and Theodoret.

Hayah, to be, become, happen, occurring over 3,500 times. God's name in verse 14 is built from it: ehyeh asher ehyeh, rendered I AM WHO I AM, which can equally be translated I will be what I will be, since the Hebrew imperfect covers present and future. The same form, ehyeh, appears in verse 12, I will be with you. Interpreters debate whether the name's main sense is God's self-existence, his freedom, or his faithful presence; the chapter makes the promise of presence the context in which the name is heard.

Qodesh, holiness, the quality of belonging to God and being set apart from common use. It occurs about 470 times, most densely in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Ezekiel. Its first appearance in the Bible is here, in admat-qodesh, ‘ground of holiness’ (verse 5), where it describes a place made holy by God's presence. Exodus will go on to build a whole order of holy space, holy objects, and holy people around that presence in the tabernacle.

Mal'akh, messenger or angel, about 210 occurrences. The word itself only means someone sent, human or divine; context decides. The phrase the angel of the LORD (verse 2) names a figure who speaks and acts for God so fully that the text moves from the angel appearing to God speaking without a break (verses 2 and 4), as in Genesis 16 and Judges 13. Stephen retells the scene with the angel (Acts 7:30, 35), and Justin Martyr identified the angel with the Son.

Seneh, a thornbush, found only six times: five in verses 2-4 and once in Deuteronomy 33:16, where God is “Him who dwelt in the burning bush”. The species cannot be identified with confidence. Its lowliness drew comment early: the Midrash (Exodus Rabbah 2:5) has Rabbi Joshua ben Korchah tell a questioner that God spoke from a thornbush to show that no place is empty of the divine presence.

'Oni, affliction, misery, about 36 occurrences. It comes from the root 'anah, ‘to oppress, humble’, used of Egypt's forced labor in 1:11-12, and it returns in verse 17, ‘I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt’. Deuteronomy 26:7 remembers the exodus in the same words, and the Passover bread is “the bread of affliction” (Deuteronomy 16:3). God's seeing of 'oni is the ground of the whole rescue.

Paqad, to attend to, inspect, visit, appoint, about 300 occurrences. It means to take note of someone and act on what is found, for blessing or for judgment. In verse 16, paqod paqadti, ‘I have surely attended to you’, echoes Joseph's dying promise, ‘God will surely attend to you’ (Genesis 50:24-25), so the elders hear the words their ancestors had carried for generations. In 20:5 the same verb describes God ‘visiting’ iniquity.

Natsal, to snatch away, rescue, or strip, about 210 occurrences. In its causative form it is one of the Old Testament's main verbs of deliverance: God has come down lehatsilo, ‘to rescue them’ (verse 8). In another form it means to strip or plunder, and verse 22 uses it of Israel taking Egypt's wealth. The play is deliberate: one act of God strips Egypt of both its slaves and its silver.

christ:
Jesus himself uses this chapter. When the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, put a riddle to him, he answered from “the burning bush in the Book of Moses”, where God says, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’, and he drew the conclusion that “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:26-27; Luke 20:37-38). The argument turns on the covenant: a God who binds his name to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths will not let death end that bond.

Stephen's speech retells the chapter at length (Acts 7:30-35) and presents Moses as a rejected deliverer whom God sent back as “ruler and redeemer”, the pattern Stephen then applies to Jesus, whom Israel's leaders also rejected. Hebrews draws a related contrast: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ “is faithful as the Son over God's house” (Hebrews 3:5-6).

The name revealed in verses 14 and 15 runs through the New Testament. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, rendered verse 14 egō eimi ho ōn, ‘I am the one who is’, and Revelation describes God as the one “who is and was and is to come” (Revelation 1:4, 8), an expansion of that Greek name. In John's Gospel Jesus says, “before Abraham was born, I am!” (John 8:58), and his hearers take up stones, apparently hearing a claim to the name. John's absolute egō eimi echoes Isaiah at least as closely as Exodus, for the Septuagint of Isaiah renders God's self-declaration ‘I am he’ (ani hu) with the same words (Isaiah 41:4; 43:10; 46:4), and so does Deuteronomy 32:39. Jesus also says that he has revealed the Father's name to his disciples (John 17:6, 26). Because the Septuagint rendered YHWH as kyrios, Lord, the earliest Christian confession, ‘Jesus is Lord’, applied the divine name's Greek form to him, and Paul can say that God gave him “the name above all names” (Philippians 2:9-11, drawing on Isaiah 45:23).

Many early Christian writers, beginning with Justin Martyr (First Apology 63; Dialogue with Trypho 59-60), read the angel of the LORD in the bush as an appearance of the Son before his incarnation, the one who both is sent and speaks as God. Others, then and now, take the angel as a created messenger speaking in God's name. The text itself stresses that in meeting the angel Moses met God, and the church has read the scene in the light of the one who is both sent by the Father and one with him. The link is theological rather than a prediction.

Most of all, the movement of the chapter, a God who sees his people's suffering and comes down to rescue them (verses 7-8), is the movement the New Testament finds completed when the Son came down from heaven to save. Isaiah had already remembered the exodus in these terms: “In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them” (Isaiah 63:9). The promise “I will surely be with you” (verse 12) is echoed in the last words of Matthew's Gospel, “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
interpretation:
Jewish reading of the chapter began early. Philo of Alexandria (On the Life of Moses 1.65-67, early first century AD) read the thornbush as a figure of the oppressed people and the fire as their oppressors, so that the bush not consumed promised that Israel would survive, and he read the Greek name ho ōn as naming true Being. The Midrash Exodus Rabbah (2:5) reports that Rabbi Joshua ben Korchah told a Gentile that God spoke from a lowly thornbush to teach that no place is empty of the divine presence. The Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 9b) reads ehyeh asher ehyeh as a promise: I will be with them in this servitude as I will be with them in their servitude to later kingdoms; Rashi repeats it in his commentary on verse 14. Maimonides (Guide of the Perplexed 1.63) took the name philosophically, as pointing to God's necessary existence, while Martin Buber and Franz Rosenzweig, in their German translation of the Bible (Exodus in 1926) and in Buber's Moses (1946), rejected metaphysical readings and rendered the name as a promise of presence, roughly ‘I will be there as whoever I will be there’.

Christian readers from the second century took the angel in the bush as the Son (Justin Martyr, First Apology 63). Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses (late fourth century) read the bush that burned without being consumed as a figure of the virgin birth, the divine light dwelling in Mary without destroying her, and from this reading grew the Eastern icon of the Mother of God as the Unburnt Bush. Augustine (Tractates on John 38) set the name of being, I AM WHO I AM, beside the name God gave for Israel's sake, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the first too high for us and the second near to us. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, q. 13, a. 11) argued that He Who Is is the most proper name of God, because God's essence is his existence, and the historian Étienne Gilson (The Spirit of Mediaeval Philosophy, 1932) called the medieval theology built on the verse a ‘metaphysics of Exodus’. Calvin's commentary on the last four books of Moses (1563) read the name more practically, as God's claim to exist of himself while all other things have their being from him.

Modern critical scholarship has asked where the name came from. The Kenite (or Midianite) hypothesis, proposed by Friedrich Wilhelm Ghillany in 1862 and developed by Bernhard Stade, Karl Budde, and H. H. Rowley, holds that Israel learned the LORD's name and worship through Moses' Midianite in-laws; Joseph Blenkinsopp revisited it in 2008. Brevard Childs's Exodus commentary (1974) combined form criticism of the call narrative with a canonical reading of the whole, and R. W. L. Moberly (The Old Testament of the Old Testament, 1992) argued that Genesis tells the patriarchs' story from the perspective of the name revealed here.

The bush has had a long public life. In 1583 the French Reformed churches, meeting in national synod at Vitré a decade after the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre, adopted a seal showing the burning bush with the words Nec tamen consumebatur (‘yet it was not consumed’) as an emblem of a persecuted church, and the Church of Scotland and many Presbyterian churches carry the same emblem. The spiritual Go Down, Moses, first published from the singing of escaped slaves in 1861, took up God's hearing of his people's cry. In the synagogue the chapter is read in Parashat Shemot (Exodus 1:1-6:1); the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1-15 on the Third Sunday in Lent in Year C and in late summer of Year A. Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Aurora Leigh (1856) contains a famous passage on every common bush afire with God.
text:
English Bibles differ most visibly in verse 14. Most render ehyeh asher ehyeh as ‘I AM WHO I AM’ (KJV ‘I AM THAT I AM’), and several (ESV, NRSV, NIV) add a footnote, ‘I will be what I will be’, because the Hebrew imperfect can refer to the future. The ancient translations divided the same way. The Septuagint has egō eimi ho ōn, ‘I am the one who is’, and makes ho ōn the short name (‘The One Who Is has sent me’); the second-century Jewish translators Aquila and Theodotion rendered it esomai hos esomai, ‘I will be who I will be’, closer to the Hebrew form; the Latin Vulgate has ego sum qui sum. Behind verse 15, the King James Version prints ‘the LORD’, while the American Standard Version (1901) printed ‘Jehovah’, a hybrid formed from the consonants YHWH and the vowels of Adonai, and a few modern versions print ‘Yahweh’.

In verse 19 the Hebrew reads literally ‘and not by a strong hand’. The Septuagint and Vulgate read ‘except by a strong hand’, and the BSB and most modern versions follow that sense (“unless a mighty hand compels him”). Others keep the Hebrew and render ‘not even under a mighty hand’, meaning Pharaoh will resist even when struck, until the last blow (11:1). In verse 22 the King James Version's ‘borrow’ misleads: the verb sha'al means to ask, and modern versions render it so. In verse 1, the KJV's ‘the backside of the desert’ renders a phrase (achar hammidbar) that means the far side or, on a Hebrew orientation facing east, the west side of the wilderness. The chapter's verse numbering is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: The holy God who sees and hears his people's suffering comes down to rescue them, sends a reluctant servant with the promise ‘I will be with you’, and gives his name so that his people may know and call on him.

outline.t: God meets Moses in the ordinary work of a failed man's exile, and the encounter begins when Moses turns aside to pay attention.
God calls Moses by name, sets a boundary around his holiness, and introduces himself by his faithfulness to the fathers.
God's compassion is active: he sees, hears, knows, comes down, and sends. His rescue is carried out through a human messenger.
The answer to ‘Who am I?’ is not self-confidence but God's presence, and the goal of the rescue is worship.
God gives his name as both a promise and a mystery: he is who he is, he will be with his people, and he is the God of their history.
God's plan works through the community's leaders and begins with a modest request that will expose Pharaoh's heart.
God foresees Pharaoh's refusal and his own victory, and promises that the oppressed will not leave empty-handed.

teach.pitfalls:
The chapter is often preached as a lesson in self-esteem, as though God's answer to ‘Who am I?’ were ‘You are more capable than you think.’ The text says the opposite: God answers with himself, ‘I will be with you’, and Moses' adequacy is never the point. A second misreading treats the burning bush as a model for private religious experience that every believer should seek. The bush is a unique commissioning at a turning point in redemptive history, not a technique; what carries over is that God speaks, calls, and keeps his promises.

Verse 14 invites two opposite errors. One reduces it to a philosophical definition cut loose from the story, as if Moses had received a lecture on being. The other dismisses any theological content and treats it as an evasive non-answer. The text holds together God's freedom, his self-existence, and his promise of presence, and a teacher should let the three stand. Preachers also sometimes claim that the Hebrew tense proves one meaning; Hebrew verb forms mark aspect more than time, so the grammar allows both ‘I am’ and ‘I will be’. Finally, avoid presenting verses 21-22 as God endorsing theft or as a charter for anyone to take what they think they are owed; the text frames the gifts as given freely by neighbors through God's favor and as a just return for unpaid labor.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on people who are suffering and wonder whether God notices. Verse 7 speaks directly to them, and it should be read slowly: God has seen, heard, and knows. It should not be used to promise a quick end to any particular suffering, since Israel had cried for a long time (2:23). The chapter also speaks to people who feel disqualified by their past. Moses had killed a man and fled, and he was eighty and a shepherd of someone else's flock when God called him. Those who have been pushed into ministries or roles by others using ‘God will be with you’ as pressure deserve care: Moses' objections are heard, answered, and even partly accommodated (4:14-16), and his reluctance is not treated as unbelief to be shamed. For people who have lived under abusive power, the chapter's picture of a God who takes the side of the oppressed against a tyrant can be a lifeline, and they should hear that God's holiness is not the same as a harsh master's distance.

hard.q: Did God tell Moses to deceive Pharaoh with a three-day request, and to take Egypt's wealth?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient. The second-century teacher Marcion and his followers, who rejected the God of the Old Testament as a lesser deity, pointed to the plundering of Egypt as proof of a God who commands fraud. The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 91a) preserves a legend in which the Egyptians sue Israel before Alexander the Great for the return of their gold and silver. Modern readers add a second charge: God tells Moses to ask for a three-day trip to sacrifice (verse 18) when the plan is for Israel to leave for good, so the request looks like a ruse, and older English versions that said Israel ‘borrowed’ the jewelry made the whole scene sound like a con.

The responses begin with the wording. The verb in verse 22 is sha'al, to ask, not to borrow, and the text never promises a return. The Egyptians give because God grants the people favor in their sight (verse 21; 12:35-36), not because they are tricked. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.30) and Tertullian (Against Marcion 2.20) answered Marcion that the gifts were a small payment of wages for generations of unpaid labor, and in the Talmud's legend Israel's advocate, Gebiha ben Pesisa, answers the Egyptian suit by presenting a counterclaim for the wages of six hundred thousand men over 430 years. Israel's own law later made the principle general: a released slave is not to be sent away empty-handed (Deuteronomy 15:13-15), and the promise to Abraham said his descendants would come out “with many possessions” (Genesis 15:14).

On the three-day request, some interpreters, including many traditional Jewish commentators, see a deliberately modest first demand that exposes Pharaoh's hardness, since God says in the next verse that Pharaoh will refuse even this; as the plagues go on, the full demand becomes plain (10:8-11). Others acknowledge that the request conceals the whole plan and judge it a legitimate strategy toward a tyrant who had ordered the murder of Israel's sons, comparable to the midwives' answer in chapter 1. Readers with a high view of Scripture are found on both sides of that question. Exodus itself leaves a further point for the reader to notice: the same gold goes into both the golden calf (32:2-4) and the tabernacle (35:22).

hard.q: Was the name YHWH new to Moses, and did Israel learn its God from the Midianites?
hard.a:
The critical case has two parts. First, Genesis uses the name YHWH freely, and Genesis 4:26 says people began to call on it in the earliest generations, yet Exodus 3:13-15 presents the name as a revelation and Exodus 6:3 says outright that God did not make himself known to the patriarchs by it. Julius Wellhausen and the documentary hypothesis explained the tension as the mark of different sources: one strand (J) uses the name from the start, while two others (E and P) hold it back until the call of Moses. Second, the Kenite or Midianite hypothesis, from Friedrich Wilhelm Ghillany (1862) through Bernhard Stade, Karl Budde, and H. H. Rowley to Joseph Blenkinsopp (2008), argues that Moses learned the LORD's worship from Jethro, pointing to the Midianite setting of this chapter, to Jethro's sacrifice and leadership of a meal before God in 18:12, to poems that bring the LORD from Seir and Teman, and to the Egyptian references to ‘the land of the Shasu of Yhw’ in the south.

The responses are several. Traditional Jewish and Christian interpreters, among them Rashi on 6:3, held that the patriarchs knew the name but had not experienced its full meaning as the God who keeps his promises, since ‘to know’ in Hebrew often means to know by experience. R. W. L. Moberly (The Old Testament of the Old Testament, 1992) argued that the name was genuinely new to Moses and that Genesis tells the patriarchal story from the perspective of the later revelation, so that the narrator uses the name the reader knows. Against the Kenite hypothesis, others note that Exodus presents the God of the bush as the God of Israel's own fathers (verses 6, 15), that Jethro's words in 18:11, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods”, sound like a newcomer's confession rather than a teacher's, and that the Soleb evidence shows only that a name like YHWH was known in the south, which fits the Bible's own memory of the LORD coming from Sinai. Jewish and skeptical historians who hold the hypothesis see it as the best explanation of the southern evidence; many Christian scholars see the same evidence as consistent with the biblical account. The question of the name's history is a second-order one on which faithful readers differ, and the chapter's own claim is clear: the God who speaks from the bush is the God who promised Abraham, now making himself known in a new way.

observe: List the verbs God uses about himself in verses 7-10. What does he say he has done, and what does he say he will do?
What two objections does Moses raise in this chapter, and how does God answer each one?
What does God predict about Pharaoh, the Egyptians, and Israel's departure in verses 18-22?
interpret: Why do you think God answers Moses' question ‘Who am I?’ with ‘I will be with you’ rather than with reassurance about Moses' abilities?
What does the name I AM WHO I AM reveal about God, and what does it withhold? Why might both matter?
Jesus used verse 6 to argue for the resurrection (Mark 12:26-27). How does God's calling himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob support that conclusion?
apply: God says he has seen, heard, and known his people's suffering. Where do you most need to trust that God sees your situation, or someone else's?
Moses had to turn aside to look at the bush before God spoke. What would it look like for you to slow down and pay attention to God in the ordinary work of this week?
Moses felt inadequate for what God asked. What task are you avoiding because you are looking at yourself rather than at the promise of God's presence?
